'''Robert Luke Devaney''' (April 9, 1948 – November 16, 2025) was an American mathematician known for his research in [[dynamical systems theory]]. He was the Feld Family Professor of Teaching Excellence at [[Boston University]] and served as the president of the [[Mathematical Association of America]] from 2013 to 2015.

Devaney's research spanned [[dynamical systems]], [[celestial mechanics]], and [[complex dynamics]]. He was among the first mathematicians to systematically study the dynamics of transcendental entire functions, and the fractal structures he described in their [[Julia set|Julia sets]] became known as ''Devaney hairs''.<ref name="Keen2010">{{citation |last=Keen |first=Linda |title=Introduction to the Robert Devaney special issue |journal=Journal of Difference Equations and Applications |volume=16 |issue=5–6 |pages=407–409 |year=2010 |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/10236190903260838 |access-date=September 12, 2026 |doi=10.1080/10236190903260838}}</ref>

==Biography==

=== Early life and education ===
Devaney was born in [[Lawrence, Massachusetts]], on April 9, 1948.<ref name=":0">{{citation |title=Robert Devaney Curriculum Vitae |url=https://math.bu.edu/people/bob/vita.pdf |access-date=December 2, 2023 |website=Mathematics Department |publisher=[[Boston University]]}}</ref> He was raised in nearby [[Methuen, Massachusetts|Methuen]], and attended [[Central Catholic High School (Massachusetts)|Central Catholic High School]].<ref name="BUMemorial">{{citation |title=Remembering Mathematician Bob Devaney |date=February 18, 2026 |website=Arts & Sciences |url=https://www.bu.edu/cas/remembering-bobdevaney/ |access-date=September 12, 2026 |publisher=[[Boston University]]}}</ref>

After high school, Devaney graduated from the [[College of the Holy Cross]] in [[Worcester, Massachusetts]], with a [[Bachelor of Arts]] in mathematics with highest honors in 1969.<ref name="pres">{{citation|url=http://www.maa.org/about-maa/governance/maa-presidents/robert-l-devaney|title=Robert L. Devaney|department=About MAA: Governance|publisher=[[Mathematical Association of America]]|accessdate=2015-09-28}}.</ref> As an undergraduate at Holy Cross, he was named the Fenwick Scholar, the college's highest academic honor.<ref name="PurplePatcher1969">{{citation |author=College of the Holy Cross |title=Purple Patcher |date=1969 |url=https://archive.org/details/purplepatcher1969coll |access-date=September 12, 2026 |at=senior class entry for Robert Luke Devaney |location=Worcester, Massachusetts |publisher=College of the Holy Cross |via=Internet Archive}}</ref> His senior undergraduate thesis, "Lens Spaces as Coset Spaces", was published in the fifth volume of the ''Pi Mu Epsilon Journal''.<ref name="DevaneyPublications">{{citation |title=Robert L. Devaney's Publications |url=https://math.bu.edu/people/bob/publications.html |access-date=September 12, 2026 |publisher=Boston University Department of Mathematics}}</ref> He then earned his [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] in mathematics in 1973 from the [[University of California, Berkeley]], under Fields medalist [[Stephen Smale]].<ref>{{mathgenealogy|id=6810}}</ref> His doctoral dissertation was titled, "Reversible diffeomorphisms and flows".<ref name="phd">
{{citation |type=PhD thesis |last=Devaney |first=Robert Luke |date=June 1973 |title=Reversible diffeomorphisms and flows |chapter= |publisher=University of California, Berkeley |oclc=21927116 |hdl= |url=https://search.library.berkeley.edu/permalink/01UCS_BER/10rhv18/alma991075871509706532 |access-date=}}
</ref>
=== Academic career ===
After completing his doctorate, Devaney was a [[Postdoctoral researcher|postdoctoral fellow]] at [[Northwestern University]] from 1974 to 1976 and an assistant professor of mathematics at [[Tufts University]] from 1976 to 1980.<ref name=":0" /> During the spring semester of 1980, he was a visiting assistant professor at the [[University of Maryland, College Park]], and that year he joined [[Boston University]] as an associate professor of mathematics.<ref name=":0" /> He served as chair of Boston University's Department of Mathematics from 1983 to 1986 and became a full professor there in 1986.<ref name=":0" /> During his career at Boston University, he also held visiting appointments at the [[Mathematical Sciences Research Institute]] in 1984 and 1989, [[Paris-Sud University]] and the [[Max Planck Institute for Mathematics]] in 1988, the [[Centre de Recerca Matemàtica]] in 2001, and the [[University of Barcelona]] in 2008.<ref name=":0" />

Beginning in 1989, Devaney directed the [[National Science Foundation]]-sponsored Dynamical Systems and Technology Project at Boston University.<ref name="BUMetcalf200322">{{citation |title=2003 Metcalf Award Winners |website=Office of the Provost |url=https://www.bu.edu/provost/awards-publications/award-opportunities/university-wide-teaching-awards/metcalf/awards-for-excellence-in-teaching/past-awardees/2003-metcalf/ |access-date=September 12, 2026 |publisher=[[Boston University]]}}</ref> The project was designed to help secondary-school and college mathematics teachers introduce contemporary subjects including [[Chaos theory|chaos]], [[Fractal|fractals]], and [[dynamical systems]] into their classrooms and to use technology in teaching those subjects.<ref name="BUDSTP22">{{citation |title=Dynamical Systems and Technology Project |url=https://math.bu.edu/DYSYS/dysys.html |access-date=September 12, 2026 |publisher=Boston University Department of Mathematics}}</ref> He also co-directed the Boston University Ordinary Differential Equations Project with mathematicians Paul Blanchard and Glen R. Hall; originally funded by two NSF grants, the project sought to incorporate modern dynamical-systems theory into the traditional sophomore-level course in [[Ordinary differential equation|ordinary differential equations]] and produced a textbook based on that approach.<ref name="BUODE22">{{citation |title=The Boston University Ordinary Differential Equations Project |url=https://math.bu.edu/odes/ |access-date=September 12, 2026 |publisher=Boston University Department of Mathematics}}</ref> Outside academia, he served as a "chaos consultant" for theatrical productions of [[Arcadia (play)|''Arcadia'']] and as a mathematical consultant for the 2007 production of the film [[21 (2008 film)|''21'']].<ref name="BUMemorial" />

In 2010, Boston University named Devaney its inaugural Feld Family Professor of Teaching Excellence.<ref name="BUFeld201022">{{citation |last=Barlow |first=Rich |title=CAS Names First Feld Family Professor |date=February 18, 2010 |website=BU Today |url=https://www.bu.edu/articles/2010/cas-names-first-feld-family-professor/ |access-date=September 12, 2026 |publisher=[[Boston University]]}}</ref> He then served as president of the [[Mathematical Association of America]] from 2013 to 2015.<ref name="MAADevaney202622">{{citation |title=Robert L. "Bob" Devaney (1948–2025): Remembering a Life of Dedicated Service to the MAA |date=January 27, 2026 |url=https://maa.org/news/robert-l-bob-devaney-1948-2025-remembering-a-life-of-dedicated-service-to-the-maa/ |access-date=September 12, 2026 |publisher=[[Mathematical Association of America]]}}</ref> He retired from Boston University in 2018, becoming a professor emeritus of mathematics there.<ref name="BUMemorial" />

Devaney died on November 16, 2025, at the age of 77.<ref>[https://www.currentobituary.com/member/obit/296756 Robert L. "Bob" Devaney]</ref>

==Mathematical research==
Devaney is known for formulating a simple and widely used definition of [[Chaos theory|chaotic systems]], one that does not need advanced concepts such as [[measure theory]].<ref>{{citation|title=Chaos: A Mathematical Introduction|volume=18|series=Australian Mathematical Society Lecture Series|first1=John|last1=Banks|first2=Valentina|last2=Dragan|first3=Arthur|last3=Jones|publisher=Cambridge University Press|year=2003|isbn=9780521531047|page=viii|bibcode=2003cmi..book.....B|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4RWUtBO_FSkC&pg=PR8|quote=Although there are several competing definitions of chaos, we concentrate here on the one given by Robert Devaney, which avoids the use of measure theory and uses only elementary notions from analysis.}}</ref> In his 1989 book ''An Introduction to Chaotic Dynamical Systems'', Devaney defined a system to be chaotic if it has [[Butterfly effect|sensitive dependence on initial conditions]], it is [[Mixing (mathematics)#Topological mixing|topologically transitive]] (for any two [[open set]]s, some points from one set will eventually hit the other set), and its [[periodic orbit]]s form a [[dense set]].<ref>{{citation|title=Modeling Complex Systems|series=Graduate Texts in Physics|first=Nino|last=Boccara|edition=2nd|publisher=Springer-Verlag|year=2010|isbn=9781441965622|page=180|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=boUorPmcbKMC&pg=PA180}}.</ref> Later, it was observed that this definition is redundant: sensitive dependence on initial conditions follows automatically as a mathematical consequence of the other two properties.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Banks | first1 = J.
 | last2 = Brooks | first2 = J.
 | last3 = Cairns | first3 = G.
 | last4 = Davis | first4 = G.
 | last5 = Stacey | first5 = P.
 | doi = 10.2307/2324899
 | issue = 4
 | journal = The American Mathematical Monthly
 | mr = 1157223
 | pages = 332–334
 | title = On Devaney's definition of chaos
 | volume = 99
 | year = 1992| jstor = 2324899
 }}.</ref>

Devaney hairs, a [[fractal]] structure in certain [[Julia set]]s, are named after Devaney, who was the first to investigate them.<ref name="keen"/><ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Rempe | first1 = Lasse
 | last2 = Rippon | first2 = Philip J.
 | last3 = Stallard | first3 = Gwyneth M. | author3-link = Gwyneth Stallard
 | doi = 10.1080/10236190903282824
 | issue = 5–6
 | journal = [[Journal of Difference Equations and Applications]]
 | mr = 2675603
 | pages = 739–762
 | title = Are Devaney hairs fast escaping?
 | volume = 16
 | year = 2010| arxiv = 0904.1403| s2cid = 14414411
 }}.</ref>

==Awards and honors==
In 1995, Devaney won the [[Deborah and Franklin Haimo Awards for Distinguished College or University Teaching of Mathematics|Deborah and Franklin Tepper Haimo Award for Distinguished University Teaching]] of the [[Mathematical Association of America]].<ref>{{citation|url=http://www.maa.org/programs/maa-awards/teaching-awards/haimo-award-distinguished-teaching/list-of-recipients|title=Deborah and Franklin Tepper Haimo Award – List of Recipients|publisher=[[Mathematical Association of America]]|accessdate=2015-09-28}}.</ref>
In 2002, Devaney won the [[National Science Foundation]] Director's Award for Distinguished Teaching Scholars.<ref name="butoday">{{citation|url=http://www.bu.edu/today/2010/cas-names-first-feld-family-professor/|title=CAS Names First Feld Family Professor: Robert Devaney makes fractals crackle, starting in high school|journal=BU Today|publisher=[[Boston University]]|first=Rich|last=Barlow|date=February 18, 2000}}.</ref><ref>{{citation|url=http://math.bu.edu/bobnsfaward.html|title=BU professor wins NSF teaching award|publisher=Boston University|date=February 2007|accessdate=2015-09-28}}.</ref>

In 2008, a conference in honor of Devaney's 60th birthday was held in [[Tossa de Mar]], [[Spain]]. The papers from the conference were published in a special issue of the ''Journal of Difference Equations and Applications'' in 2010, also honoring Devaney.<ref name="keen">{{citation
 | last = Keen | first = Linda | authorlink = Linda Keen
 | doi = 10.1080/10236190903260838
 | issue = 5–6
 | journal = Journal of Difference Equations and Applications
 | pages = 407–409
 | title = Introduction to the Robert Devaney special issue
 | volume = 16
 | year = 2010| s2cid = 121692691}}. </ref>
 
In 2012, he became one of the inaugurals [[fellow]]s of the [[American Mathematical Society]].<ref>{{citation|url=https://www.ams.org/profession/fellows-list|title=List of Fellows of the American Mathematical Society|publisher=[[American Mathematical Society]]|accessdate=2015-09-28}}</ref>

;Books

*''An Introduction to Chaotic Dynamical Systems'' (Benjamin/Cummings 1986; 2nd ed., Addison-Wesley, 1989; reprinted by Westview Press, 2003)<ref>Review of ''An introduction to chaotic dynamical systems'' by Richard C. Churchill (1987), {{MR|0811850}}.</ref><ref>Review of ''An Introduction to Chaotic Dynamical Systems'' by Philip Holmes (1987), ''SIAM Review'' 29 (4): 654–658, {{JSTOR|2031218}}.</ref><ref name="DevaneyEckmann1987">{{citation|last=Eckmann|first=Jean-Pierre|title=Review of ''An Introduction to Chaotic Dynamical Systems'' by Robert L. Devaney|journal=Physics Today|volume=40|issue=7|year=1987|page=72|issn=0031-9228|doi=10.1063/1.2820117|url=http://digitale-objekte.hbz-nrw.de/storage2/2021/12/17/file_8/9103225.pdf }}</ref>
*''The Science of Fractal Images'' (with [[Michael Barnsley|Barnsley]], [[Benoit Mandelbrot|Mandelbrot]], [[Heinz-Otto Peitgen|Peitgen]], [[Dietmar Saupe|Saupe]], and Voss, Springer-Verlag, 1988)<ref>Review of ''The Science of Fractal Images'' by P. D. F. Ion (1992), {{MR|0952853}}.</ref>
*''Chaos, Fractals, and Dynamics: Computer Experiments in Mathematics'' (Addison-Wesley, 1990)<ref>Review of ''Chaos, Fractals, and Dynamics'' by Thomas Scavo (1991), ''The College Mathematics Journal'' 22 (1): 82–84, {{doi|10.2307/2686745}}.</ref>
*''A First Course in Chaotic Dynamical Systems: Theory and Experiment'' (Addison-Wesley, 1992)<ref>Review of ''A First Course in Chaotic Dynamical Systems'' by Frederick R. Marotto (1994), {{MR|1202237}}.</ref>
*''Fractals: A Tool Kit of Dynamics Activities'' (with J. Choate and A. Foster, Key Curriculum Press, 1999)
*''Iteration: A Tool Kit of Dynamics Activities'' (with J. Choate and A. Foster, Key Curriculum Press, 1999)
*''Chaos: A Tool Kit of Dynamics Activities'' (with J. Choate, Key Curriculum Press, 2000)
*''The Mandelbrot and Julia Sets: A Tool Kit of Dynamics Activities'' (Key Curriculum Press, 2000)
*''Differential Equations'' (with P. Blanchard and G. R. Hall, 3rd ed., Brooks/Cole, 2005)
*''Differential Equations, Dynamical Systems, and an Introduction to Chaos'' (with [[Morris Hirsch]] and [[Stephen Smale]], 2nd ed., Academic Press, 2004; 3rd ed., Academic Press, 2013)<ref>Review of ''Differential Equations, Dynamical Systems, and an Introduction to Chaos'' by Michael Hurley (2005), {{MR|2144536}}.</ref>
